newsitem.title: FRANCE: ARTHUIS SAYS HAS GERMAN SUPPORT ON EMU COUNCIL.
newsitem.headline: ARTHUIS SAYS HAS GERMAN SUPPORT ON EMU COUNCIL.

text.p: France will push ahead in the next few months to win backing for a stability council to act as a counterweight to the European Central Bank after the launch of monetary union, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday.
The proposal had not yet won majority support in the European Union, he said.
"But I can assure you that our way of seeing things is totally shared by our German partners," he told a conference on the new euro currency.
"I plan to work in the next few months to widen support for this idea," he said. "It is very important that there is a political pillar to act as a counterweight in the institutional balance."
Some politicians have voiced fears that the future European Central Bank -- modelled on the independent German Bundesbank -- will exert too much power after the launch of a single currency.
In response France has proposed a "stability council" -- which could be criticised by some as a form of embryonic government -- that will co-ordinate economic policies after monetary union.
France has nothing to fear from monetary union with Germany, especially since its drive to cut public deficits has given it the credibility to make its voice heard, Arthuis said.

He also said that people should give up "fantasies" about promoting growth through manipulating the exchange rate of the future single European currency against the dollar, saying it was up to the market to set the parity.

Arthuis was speaking in a debate on monetary union in which the drive to cut budget deficits came under fire for choking growth, and where Germany in particular was accused of pushing an "austerity pact" on its European partners.
Germany has riled its partners with its tough stance on a stability pact meant to ensure future monetary union members do not run up big budget deficits after the euro has been launched.
"I will say it in a crude and direct way -- we have nothing to fear from monetary union with Germany," Arthuis told the conference at the Senate, the upper house of parliament.
"The improvement in our budgets to which we are committed allows us to negotiate with our partners in confidence."

Arthuis, who supports the stability pact in principle, nonetheless renewed criticism of a key German demand -- for a numerical definition of the exceptional circumstances under which a country would be allowed to run up a big deficit.

German insistence on a numerical definition of these circumstances threatens to torpedo agreement on the stability pact -- seen by many as a important pin to hold the whole monetary union process in place.

"It is very unwise to fix a single figure for everybody," Arthuis said, arguing that the size and effect of an economic recession -- the most likely excuse for running a high deficit -- would vary from one country to another.

Arthuis noted that Germany wanted to define temporary and exceptional circumstances as being an economic shrinkage of two percent or more. "Since the Liberation (from German occupation in 1944) France has never had such a recession."
He also said France must resist "sterile theoretical debates" on the validity of a single currency, and recognise the new euro would provide the stability needed to create jobs.
While Europe had been vulnerable before to swings in the dollar, the exchange rate would matter less after the launch of the single currency, with a big volume of goods traded in euros.
"Not long ago the Americans were saying 'the dollar is our currency and your problem'. We will be able to say 'the euro is our currency and your problem'," he said.

While he said he still believed the dollar had room to rise against the franc, it would be up to financial markets to fix the exchange rate of the dollar agaainst the new euro at the launch of monetary union in January 1999.
"The right parity is the one which allows us to have the lowest possible interest rates," he said. "It is the market which will fix the parity between the dollar and the euro."

Some economists have suggested Europe's leaders might welcome a weaker currency to breathe new life into their economies, hit by mass unemployment and -- at Germany's insistence -- a permanent commitment to curb budget deficits.
"Let's stop these fantasies about parity," Arthuis said.
